newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn plans higher borrowing in extra budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn plans higher borrowing in extra budget.

text.p: Germany announced on Friday it would draft a supplementary budget for 1997 envisaging higher new borrowing, but declined to say whether the deficit would exceed the strict targets for Europe's single currency.
Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said in a statement the supplementary budget would "make an exceptional allowance for higher new borrowing".

A Finance Ministry spokesman said "no decision has yet been taken" on the amount of extra borrowing which will be needed in the financial package to cope with the fallout of unemployment which has exceeded forecasts and tax revenue shortfalls.

The supplementary budget amounts to the last move Finance Minister Theo Waigel can make to cut the budget deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product -- the so-called "point landing" demanded by those in Germany who want the planned euro currency to be as hard as the mark.

Bonn earlier this year raised its budget deficit target for 1997 from an originally budgeted 2.5 percent to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product -- leaving precious little room to raise borrowing without missing the strict deficit goal.

The ministry spokesman declined to say whether the higher borrowing would take Germany's public sector deficit over 3.0 percent, noting that the Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union (EMU) only mentions the figure "three".

"The government will do everything possible to achieve that," the spokesman said. European leaders will decide in the first half of 1998 on which countries can join EMU on the basis of actual budget results for this year.

The powerful parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Wolfgang Schaeuble, added to the impression that Bonn wanted to use the leeway allowed by Maastricht to ensure EMU starts on time in 1999.
Schaeuble told the Stuttgarter Zeitung that he did not want to get involved in a "decimal point debate".
"The number in any given year doesn't matter that much -- rather a sustained policy of stability," he said in an interview to be published on Saturday.
But powerful figures in Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) would rather see EMU delayed rather than let it start on time in 1999 if countries overshoot the targets.
They say that fudging the criteria would let in countries like Italy, which do not have the same record of stability as Germany, and would turn the euro into a soft currency.
Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber said in a newspaper interview to be published on Saturday that not just Germany, but also France must meet the 3.0 percent deficit goal.
"The fundamental principle that stability has precedence over the timetable must count throughout Europe," Huber told the Berliner Morgenpost.
Commenting on the 1998 budget, now being drafted by Kohl's three-party coalition, Bohl said it would meet constitutional requirements that new borrowing does not exceed investment.

"With that we will fulfil the Maastricht criteria to participate in European monetary union. Through budget measures already introduced, among others privatisation, Germany will definitely meet the three percent criterion," Bohl said.
It was not immediately clear whether Bohl's comments referred to just 1998 or to 1997 as well.
News of the supplementary budget overshadowed the passage through parliament's finance committee on Friday of a separate bumper package of coalition tax reforms.
The committee made minor changes which would increase the tax burden on businesses -- especially utilities -- next year, while leaving overall net tax cuts little changed.

Net tax cuts to Germans next year will total 1.2 billion marks, while cuts in income and corporate taxes would slash the tax burden in 1999 by 44.9 billion marks. The government plans partly to offset the cuts by hiking indirect taxes.
